sourceEvidence.label: MAINFRAME stable-core execution authority source collection

assessment.summary: The source supports centralizing stable-core execution under a kernel-owned metadata-only authority, but the selected supervised route and caller migrations remain in progress.

nonNegotiables: The kernel owns durable Run, ToolCall, PolicyDecision, and Evidence identity for stable-core execution.
The ledger and Evidence never retain raw input, stdout, stderr, or a raw broker envelope.
Raw input and result values use bounded owner-private transient channels.
A running or terminal correlation is never automatically re-executed.
A terminal retry may return result_available=false when the transient result is unavailable.
Unsupported non-shell routes remain unverified without qualifying interception evidence.
assumptions: No measured latency, memory, or concurrency budget was supplied.
The incremental design must work without installing a permanent service.
Owner-private transport narrows accidental and cross-user exposure but is not a same-user sandbox.
The reviewed stable-core contract remains the only execution inventory in scope.

opportunities.title: Centralize stable-core execution authority
opportunities.summary: Move reservation, policy, fixed execution, terminal recovery, and metadata-only Evidence behind one kernel-owned boundary.
opportunities.diagnosis: Caller-local sequencing splits intent, execution, retry, and durable Evidence across processes, so crashes and adapter drift can make replay safety and authority ambiguous.

evidence.claim: Lines 583-630 introduce a fixed hidden broker grammar and a public durable bridge, while lines 2855-2860 fail closed before broad legacy dispatch; these are drifting worktree bytes.
Lines 48-66, 124-138, and 177-350 bound and clean caller-side temporary transport around the control-plane route.
Lines 170-185, 307-348, 475-493, and 2475-2577 model canonical metadata, metadata-only broker receipts, transient result delivery, and interrupted recovery without replay.
Lines 31-198 implement bounded owner-private consume-once input and result files bound to the durable request.
Lines 57-104 and 179-454 fix executable, argv, environment, process group, deadline, cancellation endpoint, and capture bounds without providing an OS sandbox.
Lines 47-139 bind a per-correlation worker, consume transient input, drive policy/execution, publish transient output, and refuse to retry running or terminal calls.
Lines 245-317 and 347-433 bind retries to canonical reservation, supervise a worker, recover an unresponsive running call, and expose result_available separately from terminal outcome.
Lines 623-726, together with skills/pi/extensions/mainframe.ts:2487-2567, retain caller-specific invocation and broker-envelope handling, so both migrations remain open.
Lines 44-65, 69-124, and 143-215 keep evidence levels route-specific and do not promote shell-only evidence into non-shell enforcement.
Line 147 still expects a durable broker_envelope while the collected kernel persists broker_receipt, establishing source/test drift rather than a passing gate.
Because reservation, execution, and recording are sequenced by independent caller processes, caller-local coordination cannot eliminate every execution-versus-Evidence crash window.
A long-lived authority could centralize queueing and lifecycle further, but the collected source does not establish sufficient demand or actual isolated-worker support.

desiredInvariants: The kernel durably binds one correlation to one canonical request, Run, ToolCall, policy decision, and terminal Evidence chain.
The durable chain contains metadata and cryptographic bindings only; raw input, stdout, stderr, and broker envelopes remain transient.
Only a fixed reviewed executable, argv, environment, workspace, deadline, and output bound can execute.
Running and terminal requests are never automatically re-executed.
A terminal retry can safely report result_available=false without implying that execution did not occur.
Host and release claims never exceed their qualifying evidence.

options.title: Caller-local sequencing around the legacy broker
options.summary: Have every adapter reserve, invoke, and append records in its own process.

evidenceCoverage.rationale: The fixed hidden grammar narrows the leaf route, but local sequencing still owns the durable boundary.
MCP and Pi would each retain duplicated sequencing and need direct bounds while migration is pending.
No caller-local sequence can close the cross-process crash window.

tradeoffs.assessment: Exact local guards narrow misuse, but authority and Evidence still drift between callers.
tradeoffs.validationPlan: Fault-inject every caller between reserve, broker spawn, completion, and record append; reject the option if any state permits ambiguous replay.

tradeoffs.assessment: No new supervisor or service hop is required beyond existing caller and broker work.
tradeoffs.validationPlan: Measure p50/p95 end-to-end latency for the current public invoke path as the baseline.

tradeoffs.assessment: Only current caller and broker buffers are retained, subject to existing bounds.
tradeoffs.validationPlan: Measure peak RSS and captured bytes for maximum-size stable-core results.

tradeoffs.assessment: A crash can leave execution completion and durable recording inconsistent, making retry safety ambiguous.
tradeoffs.validationPlan: Use an execution counter under crash injection and require deterministic recovery without a second execution.

tradeoffs.assessment: Each adapter needs separate diagnostics, reconciliation, and drift control.
tradeoffs.validationPlan: Inventory adapter-specific state machines and compare their error/result schemas for exact parity.

tradeoffs.assessment: This preserves current caller shapes and has the smallest immediate migration, but defers the structural change.
tradeoffs.validationPlan: Run existing compatibility suites while confirming no new route or state format is introduced.

residualRisks: Reservation, execution, and Evidence are not one authority boundary.
Adapter-specific retry and policy logic can drift.
Raw values cross more caller-owned paths.

workPackages: Keep fixed broker grammar and per-route bounds as tactical protections.
acceptanceCriteria: This baseline is not accepted as the terminal architecture.
migrationNotes: Retain only during bounded migration to the selected route.
implementationReadiness.rollback: Restore the last reviewed legacy release only as a stopgap; do not claim centralized authority.

options.title: Per-request kernel reservation and supervised fixed executor
options.summary: Reserve exact identities in the kernel, execute through a fixed short-lived supervisor, keep raw values transient, and persist metadata-only Evidence.

evidenceCoverage.rationale: The kernel becomes the durable identity, outcome, recovery, and Evidence owner.
Bounded consume-once transport keeps raw values outside durable state.
Fixed supervision narrows process invocation but does not provide strong sandbox isolation.
The worker refuses to execute a running or terminal correlation again.
MCP and Pi migrations are still required, so their current paths need tactical bounds.
Drifting test expectations must be reconciled before completion can be evaluated.
Kernel reservation and terminal Evidence replace the caller-local crash boundary.

tradeoffs.assessment: Identity, policy, fixed execution, and metadata-only Evidence converge in one kernel-owned flow; raw values remain transient. Same-user IPC and non-sandboxed process risk remain.
tradeoffs.validationPlan: Prove exact binding and fixed execution, scan ledger bytes for secret sentinels, and run same-user path/mode/link tamper cases.

tradeoffs.assessment: Each call adds reservation/ledger synchronization, transient-file operations, a worker spawn, and supervision.
tradeoffs.validationPlan: Compare p50/p95/p99 public-invoke latency for representative small and maximum inputs against the legacy baseline; set the threshold before release.

tradeoffs.assessment: A bounded worker and bounded pipe capture exist per active request, but no resident service is introduced.
tradeoffs.validationPlan: Measure peak combined RSS and buffered bytes at one and the maximum supported concurrent call count; reject unbounded growth.

tradeoffs.assessment: At-most-once execution and terminal recovery remove ambiguous replay. Raw-result availability intentionally regresses after result consumption or loss, yielding result_available=false.
tradeoffs.validationPlan: Fault-inject every lifecycle boundary, assert the execution counter remains one, and verify terminal retries return metadata without replay when the result is absent.

tradeoffs.assessment: Durable identities, receipts, and recovery improve local diagnosis, while unavailable-result reconciliation and transient cleanup need explicit tooling.
tradeoffs.validationPlan: Exercise operator lookup and cleanup workflows for success, denial, timeout, cancellation, interrupted execution, and lost results.

tradeoffs.assessment: Bash, MCP, Pi, and tests must converge on one closed result contract and remove direct legacy authority paths.
tradeoffs.validationPlan: Add direct-path negative tests per adapter and require clean candidate plus installed-candidate parity before promotion.

residualRisks: A compromised same-user process may still target owner-private transient paths or sockets.
The supervised subprocess is constrained but not sandboxed.
A consumed or lost raw result is intentionally unavailable even though durable terminal metadata remains.
MCP and Pi remain migration seams until their direct paths are removed.

workPackages: Finish transient lifecycle and supervisor recovery.
Pass clean candidate, installed candidate, and separate release gates.
acceptanceCriteria: Fault-injection execution counters never exceed one per correlation.
Secret sentinels and raw envelopes never appear in the durable ledger or Evidence.
Terminal retries can return result_available=false and never replay.
All supported callers use the kernel-owned route and direct routes fail closed.
migrationNotes: Land public CLI/Bash first, then MCP, then Pi.
Keep unsupported non-shell and absent live/release claims unverified.
implementationReadiness.rollback: Disable stable-core invocation or restore the last reviewed release; never fall back from a failed kernel binding to direct broker execution.

options.title: Owner-private long-lived daemon with isolated workers
options.summary: Put policy, dispatch, cancellation, recovery, and metadata Evidence in a resident owner-private service that launches isolated short-lived workers.

evidenceCoverage.rationale: The daemon can host the existing kernel identity and metadata model.
The same privacy invariant can be carried over, but daemon-safe transient IPC is new work.
Fixed execution is reusable, but isolated-worker enforcement has not been demonstrated.
The foundational benefit remains hypothetical until load, lifecycle, and isolation evidence exists.

tradeoffs.assessment: One resident authority can reduce caller trust and add real worker isolation, but the daemon becomes a high-value target and no isolation mechanism is selected or proven.
tradeoffs.validationPlan: Threat-model peer identity, upgrades, socket access, daemon compromise, and platform isolation; run platform-specific escape tests before making an isolation claim.

tradeoffs.assessment: Kernel startup may be amortized, while IPC, queueing, and worker isolation add costs whose balance depends on concurrency.
tradeoffs.validationPlan: Benchmark serial and concurrent workloads against Option 2, comparing p50/p95/p99 latency and throughput at a predeclared concurrency threshold.

tradeoffs.assessment: A resident daemon, queue, health state, and worker bookkeeping create the highest steady-state footprint.
tradeoffs.validationPlan: Measure idle RSS, per-worker growth, queue growth under backpressure, and post-load return to baseline.

tradeoffs.assessment: Central backpressure can improve recovery, while daemon crashes, stale sockets, upgrades, and client/server skew create new availability modes.
tradeoffs.validationPlan: Run crash/restart, upgrade/downgrade, stale-socket, queue saturation, and split-version campaigns without duplicate execution.

tradeoffs.assessment: Installation, service lifecycle, health, upgrades, recovery, privacy-safe logging, and cross-platform launch integration become permanent responsibilities.
tradeoffs.validationPlan: Prototype install/start/upgrade/rollback on supported macOS and Linux hosts and measure manual recovery steps.

tradeoffs.assessment: All clients need a versioned IPC protocol, dual-route rollout, state adoption, and fallback rules.
tradeoffs.validationPlan: Prove mixed-version compatibility and rollback from a staged daemon candidate without enabling legacy execution fallback.

residualRisks: The daemon becomes an availability dependency and a high-value same-user target.
A private socket does not itself provide sandbox isolation.
Cross-platform service lifecycle and upgrade recovery remain unproven.

workPackages: Threat-model and prototype a versioned owner-private protocol.
Select and prove platform-specific worker isolation.
acceptanceCriteria: Option 3 is not accepted without measured need and isolation evidence.
migrationNotes: Revisit only if Option 2 startup, concurrency, or lifecycle measurements fail declared thresholds.
implementationReadiness.rollback: Stop the daemon and return to the proven Option 2 public route using compatible metadata state; never fall back to caller-local execution.

opportunities.recommendation: Select the supervised kernel under the current balanced constraints because it closes the authority and at-most-once gap without a resident service; keep its status in progress until tests, MCP/Pi migration, clean candidate, and installed evidence are complete.

openQuestions: What bounded cleanup horizon should apply to an unconsumed transient result?
How should CLI, MCP, and Pi present terminal result_available=false without triggering automatic replay?
Which same-user attacker capabilities are in scope for transient files and Unix sockets?
What measured concurrency or startup threshold would justify the daemon option?
